rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — it combines an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveller abuse case. The 2018 penal code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, a provision that extends to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the national police force announced arrests of transgender women after private-party photos circulated on social media; an international human-rights organisation documented further arrests and convictions under the provision.

Most concretely for travellers: in February 2024 a foreign non-binary traveller arriving at the capital's airport on a tourist visa was pulled aside while friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. They publicly warned other members of the community not to travel to countries like this one.

Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the same code, so partner travel carries the same exposure; consensual same-sex activity risks prosecution for foreign nationals too. The consequence axis of an arrest is documented rather than hypothetical: in September 2018 a local court sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and a fine of OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and publishing the photos, and two further men to three years with the same fine for featuring in the video — the judicial outcome of the January 2018 police arrests under a penal-code provision penalising appearing in female clothing or demeanour. A gender-nonconforming visitor detected on arrival can therefore be jailed, and nothing in the sources records where inside the prison system such prisoners are held.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Comparison context: sources note the explicit anti-trans statute is unusual in its region, and the traveller's public warning told others not to travel to countries like this one. The national enforcement pattern is active — the 2018 arrests were publicly announced after private-party photos circulated on social media, showing active monitoring of gender non-conformity.

The September 2018 sentences completed the documented enforcement loop: eight months after the January 2018 police arrests, a preliminary court convicted the four men under a provision of the July 2018 penal code — which allows up to one year's imprisonment and an OMR 3,000 fine for "any male that appears in female clothing or demeanor" — with the stiffer three- and four-year sentences carrying additional charges for publishing immoral acts on social media. Court-ordered imprisonment of gender-nonconforming people is the recorded pattern, not an isolated event.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The current sources record no resident-specific facts beyond the enforcement pattern already described in the summary — the 2018 arrests and the anti-trans statute apply to residents and visitors alike; no local cultural or resident-life facts are documented.

The four men sentenced in September 2018 were residents, and their convictions document how the state/province treats gender-nonconforming people inside its criminal system and what its courts order by way of imprisonment and fines — a pattern a detained visitor would meet from the inside.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Political restrictions and labour conditions affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

Unresolved: the airport account rests on a single traveller's first-hand account and could not be independently verified from the current sources, and whether the anti-trans statute has been applied at border entry for other travellers is not documented beyond that reported incident.

Prison axis: no national rule, practice or case is documented on where trans or gender-nonconforming prisoners are housed — nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, no special units, and no solitary or segregation practice. That absence cannot be read as a protected standard in a country that criminalises cross-dressing and has jailed people for it.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: not retrievable at research time (403); the underlying international legal-aid organisation's country profile documents criminalisation of same-sex activity and gender expression.

Two rights organisations' joint submission (6 Aug 2025) to a UN human-rights review: systemic legal and institutional discrimination against transgender people; recent legislative developments have deepened criminalisation of gender expression; legal gender recognition is banned and gender-affirming healthcare explicitly banned; earlier review recommendations on gender identity, expression and health access reportedly ignored; the submission calls for ending criminalisation, adopting an anti-discrimination law and permitting legal recognition.

A rights organisation's statute-level extraction from the 2018 penal code: public indecency (10 days-3 months plus an OMR 100-300 fine), impersonating or entering women-only venues disguised (1 month-1 year), producing or sharing content 'violating public morals' offline and online (up to 1 year / 10 days-1 month), plus 2011 cyber-crime provisions used against LGBT expression (1 month-3 years plus OMR 100-3,000); gender non-conformity punished through the impersonation provision.

A legal-information platform (3 Jun 2026): all same-sex conduct criminalised with up to 3 years under the 2018 penal code; prosecution often triggered by digital evidence discovered during unrelated investigations and without a family complaint; deportation is required for foreign nationals convicted of a felony (permanent) and allowed for lesser offences (3-15 years); the national telecom operator enables surveillance; outing carries social and criminal risk; assembly and advocacy restricted through the associations law.

A visitor-facing incident (27 Feb 2023): a foreign genderqueer/non-binary visitor arriving at the capital's international airport on a 10-day tourist visa says friends cleared immigration but she was held for a separate examination, made to remove her shirt and touched inappropriately by officers — direct first-hand evidence of border treatment of visibly gender-nonconforming visitors.

An international human-rights organisation's open letter (13 Jul 2020): arrests and convictions under the 2018 provision 'imitating the opposite sex'; the national police force announced arrests of 'men in women's clothing' after photos from a private party circulated on social media; enforcement also documented against a foreign expatriate in full-body covering at a women-only park hour — showing active enforcement of the cross-dressing offence against gender non-conformity.

An international human-rights organisation's regional report (16 Apr 2018): the 2018 penal code added a provision punishing any man who 'appears to dress in women's clothing', alongside a regional comparison with another country's imitation law, and records existing criminalisation of same-sex conduct and barriers to LGBT organising.

A law-journal article (2012) distinguishing homosexual acts from homosexual persons: in some countries guided by religious law, acts are criminalised (even capitally) while identity alone is not — scholarly context for the country's legal-religious framework.

A local news outlet (19 Sep 2018), on the public prosecution's announcement: a preliminary court sentenced two men to four years in jail and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and sharing photos of themselves in women's clothes on social media, and two further men to three years with the same fine for featuring in the video; the sentences fall under a July 2018 penal-code provision under which 'any male that appears in female clothing or demeanor' may be fined up to OMR 3,000 and jailed up to one year, with additional 'publishing immoral acts on social media' charges. The article notes these follow January 2018 arrests by the national police force of a group of men for dressing as women after social-media photos circulated. It documents court-ordered imprisonment of gender-nonconforming people but contains no information on where inside the prison system those convicted were housed.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country is one of the region's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. A 2018 comprehensive law for trans people provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a public-sector employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (the region's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among the region's safest (an international peace index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (an independent democracy assessment). However, a 29-year-old trans woman was shot dead in her home in the capital in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital and a public bank. The same independent democracy assessment notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, and the capital is welcoming. Even the custody consequence axis is comparatively benign: at a 2023 parliamentary hearing the national rehabilitation agency's director stated that a trans person entering the prison system has the right to decide whether to go to a men's or women's prison, trans women are currently placed in women's prisons, and a dedicated trans sector was planned for a new prison in the capital — though he conceded the gap: "the laws are very advanced here, but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line."
rewrites.blindTangential:
Same-sex marriage legal since 2013 (the region's first) — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

Prison-policy signals: the commitment to a dedicated trans sector in the planned capital prison came with the parliamentary commissioner for the prison system calling it "good news for a very vulnerable population" and estimating it would be ready in less than two years, and the rehabilitation agency told parliament that a new women's prison would for the first time account for the trans population — announced infrastructure, not yet delivered.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The self-declaration legal gender recognition, reparation pension, and public-sector employment quota under the 2018 law are resident-facing; the killing of the trans woman and the hospital and bank discrimination incidents concerned residents.

Custody practice is resident-facing: official figures from the parliamentary commissioner's office count 28 trans women and nine trans men among tens of thousands of people deprived of liberty; trans women are currently placed in female prisons, cohabitation is described as entailing "a whole process" of adaptation, and the planned trans sector of a new prison in the capital would serve people already inside the system — a visitor meets all of this only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
General crime is very low; no trans-specific travel advisory.
Prison axis: the dedicated trans sector and the new women's-prison accommodation were commitments announced in July 2023 (commissioner's estimate: ready within two years); nothing in the current sources documents whether delivery has occurred, and no source records special-unit or solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners beyond the planned sector.
blindSourceSummaries: A rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide, legal gender recognition possible, LGBTI organisations registrable; intersex bodily-autonomy protections flagged incomplete. The current civil-rights baseline a trans visitor enters.

Full text of the 2018 comprehensive law for trans people (26 Oct 2018): guaranteed identity, health and anti-discrimination rights for trans persons — the statutory backbone of the country's trans-protection regime.

A legal-status tracking platform's grid for the main city (governed by national law): marriage, legal gender change, non-discrimination, conversion-therapy ban and equal age of consent all legal/protected; hate-crime rules cover sexual orientation and gender identity.
An official government announcement: the executive promulgated the 2018 comprehensive law for trans persons — official confirmation the statute entered into force.
An independent democracy assessment 2024: Free, 96/100 (political rights 40/40, civil liberties 56/60) — strong general rights climate for trans visitors.

A trans-remembrance project's 2025 record: a 29-year-old trans woman shot dead in her home in the capital on 28 Jul 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to 7 years for the murder — documented lethal violence against a trans person with judicial follow-through.

A local news outlet (May 2024): a trans health-service user denounced mistreatment and discrimination at a hospital; criminal complaint pending, the hospital director pledged an administrative investigation after the judicial stage; local officials pressed for health-system updates.

A news outlet: a trans woman sued a public bank over discriminatory handling by a security guard and alleges the bank withheld key camera footage; a prosecutor compelled the bank to produce the material; she says she was dismissed after publicising the case.

A news outlet (28 Dec 2007): the country became the region's first to recognise same-sex civil unions — the national leader signed the law giving couples cohabiting 5+ years rights equivalent to marriage (historical baseline).

A news outlet (29 Jul 2023), citing national authorities and officials: a new prison planned for the capital will include a specific sector for the trans population, which the parliamentary commissioner for the prison system called 'good news for a very vulnerable population' and estimated would be ready in less than two years. The director of the national rehabilitation agency told a parliamentary hearing that 'if the trans person enters the system they have the right to decide if they want to go to a men's or women's prison', and that while trans women are currently placed in female prisons, cohabitation entails 'a whole process' of adaptation; he also noted a new women's prison would for the first time account for the trans population, adding 'the laws are very advanced here, but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line.' Official figures count 28 trans women and nine trans men among tens of thousands of people deprived of liberty.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is broadly workable — described as one of the most tolerant countries in the region toward sexual minorities. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the 2015 civil code was a landmark recognising transgender people's right to change their legal gender. However, the law implementing that recognition has been stalled for over eight years — the right exists on paper but not in practice. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.

No trans-specific killing has been documented here. Conversion efforts are documented, and healthcare discrimination is a significant barrier — trans people face stigma and "red tape" in accessing care, and trans-competent providers are scarce.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, unrestricted bathroom access, and no criminalisation — but the stalled recognition means no practical gender-marker change on documents. This country is under one-party authoritarian rule, where an international human-rights organisation finds that "rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice"; a UN development agency is actively engaged on trans-rights strategies. If a visitor is detained, the documented custody picture is structural and thin: as of a January 2015 reform proposal — never enacted — the prison system had no housing wing matched to gender identity, so transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, and no enacted outcome or newer documented placement practice was found in two search rounds.
rewrites.blindTangential:
No trans-specific killing has been documented here, in contrast to several neighbouring countries. The September 2025 cancellations of the flagship Pride march and other LGBTQ events in the largest city — a national-level policy signal that may colour a visit — are adjacent climate rather than a direct travel restriction.

The January 2015 separate-jails proposal is the only prison-axis document in the sources: a research institute asked the public-security ministry to house homosexual and transgender prisoners apart from the general population to protect them from sexual harassment, citing subnational statistics from another country that 67% of such prisoners had suffered sexual harassment and a 2014 survey in which most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails — a reform bid with no enacted outcome recorded.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The stalled recognition law, the documented conversion efforts, and the healthcare discrimination barriers are resident-facing — these govern residents' access to recognition, safety, and care rather than a visitor's experience.

The placement finding concerns resident prisoners: in 2015 the only housing options documented for transgender prisoners were solitary confinement or the general population, because no wing matched their gender identity, and a 2014 survey found most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails — resident-facing conditions a visitor meets only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Political controls of one ruling party, arbitrary detention of dissidents, and typhoon or monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the practical effect of the stalled recognition law on border document checks is not documented in the sources.

Prison axis: the placement finding (solitary confinement or general population only, no identity-matched wing) dates from January 2015 and comes from a never-enacted reform proposal; two search rounds found no enacted outcome and no newer documented placement practice, so today's practice is unknown — and that unknown cannot be read as a protected standard in a country with no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.
blindSourceSummaries: A foreign public broadcaster (late Sep/Oct 2025): the largest city abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other 2025 Pride events — a regional human-rights official called it worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against the country's long regional-tolerance reputation; notes the 2015 lifting of the same-sex-marriage ban left unions still without legal recognition.

An international LGBTIQ organisation's country overview (updated Mar 2026): the law granting official transgender recognition promised for 2017 still not implemented — obstacles to gender-affirming care and legal gender-marker change persist; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of Feb 2026. Same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts but confer no rights; LGBTIQ organisations operate openly though under government surveillance; the health ministry declared (Aug 2022) same-sex attraction and trans identity are not mental disorders; no law against non-consensual intersex medical interventions.

An international human-rights organisation's 2025 country report: LGBTI people's rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice; sits alongside wider repression — vague penal-code provisions used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025, proposed press-law source-disclosure rules; the country re-elected to a UN human-rights body until 2028.

A research-institute study (Oct 2024): exploration of the lived experiences of conversion efforts among LGBTIQ people — documents the experiences and forms of such efforts and includes a comprehensive data-needs analysis.

A UN country-team feature (30 Nov 2024): transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters ('Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?'), heightened scrutiny, and economic/stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence — especially for trans women in outlying provinces and ethnic minorities; framed as a case for accessible legal recognition.

A local news site (Jun 2023): a Nov 2015 milestone let people who changed gender apply for civil-status change and set out legal gender recognition, but implementing guidance stalled — policy gaps persist, same-sex marriage legal but unrecognised; four trans residents describe respectful healthcare providers undone by administrative red tape.

A foreign refugee-board information request (30 Jun 2022): no discrimination protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds; a multi-source treatment briefing covering society and authorities in the largest cities across education, employment, housing and health care.

Government media (Nov 2018): the national assembly was expected to discuss a draft law protecting transgender people's legal status and rights, targeting completion by 2020 — the law never materialised; per a rights organisation (Feb 2026) a recognition draft law was still under consideration seven years later.

A local news site (16 Jan 2015) reports a proposal by a research institute to the public-security ministry to house homosexual and transgender prisoners in jails separate from the general population to protect them from sexual harassment; the institute cited subnational statistics from another country that 67% of such prisoners had suffered sexual harassment and a 2014 survey finding that most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails. Under then-current prison infrastructure, transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population — no housing wing matched to the prisoner's gender identity existed — and the institute asked that prisoners be allowed to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome or newer documented placement practice was found in two search rounds.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The nation is among the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. It has ranked first for LGBTI legal rights in its region every year since 2015: gender identity and expression are protected from discrimination in law, legal gender recognition works by self-determination, and 'X' gender markers are available on passports. Conversion therapy is banned and the constitution guarantees LGBTI equality.

The nation records one of the lowest rates of physical or sexual victimisation of LGBTIQ+ people in its region, and the national police force has adopted hate-crime procedures for sexual-orientation and gender-identity incidents. A foreign government's diplomatic guidance describes the country as a safe environment for foreign LGBT travellers, and no government travel advisory flags trans-specific concerns.

Residual risks are minor: non-physical harassment (including online) is more common than violence and tends to be under-reported, and — in the unlikely event of arrest — prison practice has been found to lag the country's progressive law. The lag is documented, with an improving record: in May 2018 the civil court awarded seven transgender inmates of a prison €5,000 each after finding the authorities had "knowingly and repeatedly" held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers and suffered insults and "continuous sexual abuse and violence"; since the 2013 gender-law reform, trans and gender-diverse inmates transfer to the female section and now receive individual cells there, though a 2024 university study still records misgendering by officers and clothing and healthcare gaps.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Litigation flux at the border: in July 2025 an international-court intervention was filed concerning an LGBTI asylum seeker detained on arrival in 2023 and facing a removal order — direct evidence of how LGBTI arrivals are treated at the borders of the nation, though an asylum context rather than the ordinary visitor pass-through, and its outcome is pending.

The 2018 damages ruling is the prison-axis legal record: the civil court awarded each of the seven women €4,000 for breach of rights and €1,000 for damage to personal dignity, ordered the director of prisons to pay, and a human-rights NGO represented the claimants — a binding judicial finding that prison authorities knowingly and repeatedly placed the inmates at high risk of sexual and psychological violence, with transfer to the female section refused in practice because it would cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The self-determination legal gender recognition regime and passport 'X' markers are resident-facing administrative law; the prison healthcare and placement gaps concern resident inmates, with institutional practice found out of sync with national gender-identity law. A regional residents' survey ranks workers here top for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

The custody record concerns residents: the seven 2018 claimants stayed in the male section because transfer to the female section would cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, while female inmates and warders were said to be hostile; current practice — transfer to the female section with individual cells, following earlier segregation in a separate dormitory (staff rationale: "the risks of pregnancies") — governs resident inmates, not visitors.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Petty crime around nightclubs and tourist spots, and general regional terrorism guidance, are ordinary travel risks that affect everyone.

Routine border handling of trans visitors is not documented beyond the asylum-seeker case, and no source describes visa or document scrutiny for trans visitors specifically.

Prison axis: the 2024 study rests on four interviews spanning 25 years; the earlier separate-dormitory segregation is documented from that study alone; no source in this record documents current solitary or special-unit practice for trans prisoners beyond what the study describes, and the abuse documented in the 2018 ruling predates the post-2013 reform practice.
blindSourceSummaries: A regional rights map country page for the nation with the compliance breakdown across asylum, civil-society space, intersex bodily integrity, legal gender recognition, hate crime/hate speech and equality-body categories, scored per category on the map's red-to-green scale.

Data pages for the nation: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation and gender identity, discrimination illegal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. 84% rate it a 'good place' for gay people; but residents rank top of 30 regional units for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

Legal-status source: same-sex conduct legal since 29 January 1973; civil unions since 2014 and same-sex marriage since 2017; gender change without surgery; full adoption since 2014; open military service; discrimination protections cover sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics.

Academic chapter (2025): the nation records one of the lowest sexual-orientation and gender-identity physical/sexual victimisation rates in the region, yet LGBTIQ+ people still report a higher share of harassment and online hatred, and reporting of violence to the police force remains significantly low despite institutional reforms.

A university dissertation (2024): interviews with current and former transgender inmates (a 25-year cohort) found healthcare, legislative and knowledge gaps plus post-release problems, with institutional practice out of sync with national gender-identity legislation — institutional lag beneath the strong statute book.

An international-court intervention (30 Jul 2025): observations were filed in a case in which an LGBTI asylum seeker detained on arrival in April 2023 received a return decision and removal order in May 2024; the submissions raise international human-rights provisions on non-refoulement, detention conditions and individualised assessment before detention. Direct evidence of how LGBTI arrivals are treated at the nation's borders.

News report (15 Apr 2014): the elected legislature approved a constitutional amendment naming gender identity — the first in its region to do so — and introduced civil unions in the same sitting; a trans-rights organisation was among the first to applaud gender identity as a protected ground in the highest legal text.

News report (29 May 2018): the civil court awarded seven transgender inmates of a prison €5,000 each (€4,000 for breach of rights plus €1,000 for damage to personal dignity) after the prison authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers (often forgoing washing) and suffered insults and 'continuous sexual abuse and violence'. The court found the authorities had 'knowingly and repeatedly' placed them in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and female inmates and warders were said to be hostile, so they stayed in the male section. The director of prisons was ordered to pay; a human-rights NGO represented the seven women.

A university master's dissertation (2024) interviewing four current and former transgender/gender-diverse inmates of the corrections service, a cohort spanning the last 25 years: after the 2013 gender-law reform, institutional practice allowed transgender and gender-diverse inmates to transfer to the female section, whereas earlier practice had segregated them in a separate dormitory (staff described the rationale as 'the risks of pregnancies'); participants now receive individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers (masculine birth names), gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare gaps, and institutional practice lags the progressive national gender-identity law. It also cites the 2018 newspaper report of seven transgender and gender-diverse inmates winning a court award after rights breaches including strip searches, showering-privacy issues and being treated as males.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The nation is a very safe destination for transgender visitors: official 2026 Pride guidance confirms visas and entry depend only on nationality, not gender identity, passports with amended or "X" gender markers are accepted, and no medical documentation is needed at the border. Discrimination based on gender identity is prohibited by law, and since July 2025 a discriminatory motive is a statutory aggravating factor that can increase penalties by up to a third.

Practical safety supports are strong: the capital operates dedicated reporting networks for LGBTQIA+ incidents, the mayor and police committed to priority investigation of Pride-period incidents for 2026, and the capital is among the safer cities in the region for ordinary crime. Same-sex marriage is legal and non-binary people are recognised, so a trans traveller's partner status raises no border or legal problems.

The genuine caution is rising reported hostility: discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people reached 4,800 last year, up 51% in a year for transgender-specific reports and 81% since 2022, and many queer residents avoid public displays of affection. For a visitor this chiefly means a risk of harassment or verbal abuse, particularly late at night, rather than systematic danger. If a visitor is nonetheless detained, the custody consequence axis is a documented legal gap: no statute or regulation governs where transgender detainees are held — the penitentiary principles legislation separates only male and female detainees — and the prison service places detainees by the gender designation in municipal records plus case-by-case factors (including the detainee's own preference), with transgender detainees frequently held on an "extra-care facility" wing alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders; courts have treated a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier, and a February 2024 human-rights lawyers' advisory called the unregulated placement "worrying and undesirable".
rewrites.blindTangential:
National policy turbulence is pending rather than in force: a self-identification gender-recognition bill was withdrawn in July 2025 though debate restarted in December, and the non-binary "X" marker is available only through a court procedure taking 3-9 months; neither currently changes the border or discrimination rules a visitor faces.

Comparative context: the nation ranks #13 on a comparative rights map and #2 of 121 regions as a "good place", with public support at 52%; at the same time there is no statutory definition of "hate crime" at national level, the police recording hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through a dedicated expertise centre.

Custody-policy flux: the national human-rights lawyers' committee advised the caretaker minister for legal protection in February 2024 that no law, regulation or official policy governs transgender detainees' placement; the prison service confirmed placement by municipal-record gender plus case-by-case factors, the custodial-institutions agency said it was drafting guidelines that remained unpublished as of the sources, and the advisory urged rules aligned with regional human-rights standards — policy in motion rather than in force.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The legal gender-recognition process still requires an expert letter, falling short of self-determination: the self-identification bill was withdrawn in July 2025 though debate restarted in December, and the non-binary "X" marker is available only through a court procedure taking 3-9 months — all resident-facing.

Resident-facing victimisation data: official figures record that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people report physical or sexual violence (17% of trans respondents, 22% of intersex people), a third of police discrimination reports in 2022 concerned sexual orientation, only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination were recorded last year, and surveys indicate many queer residents avoid public displays of affection.

The placement practice governs detained residents: the documented cases include a trans woman first held on a regular male wing at arrival, then moved to an extra-care facility wing; a 2016 parole-board appeals ruling on a trans woman placed in a men's institution before transfer to a women's prison, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation while there; and 2017 and 2020 sentencing rulings treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier — a visitor meets this only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Pickpocketing, bike theft and taxi scams are general tourist risks affecting everyone, including in the capital.

Unresolved: the reporting platform describes its Pride-period figure (70+ reports) as "only a fraction of the total", so true incident volume is unverified; the documented enforcement gap (six convictions against 4,800 reports) is real but its practical effect on visitors is unquantified.

Prison axis: there are no official figures on the number of transgender detainees in the country, the frequency of extra-care facility placement is unquantified, and the guidelines the custodial-institutions agency was drafting as of February 2024 remain unpublished in the sources — current placement decisions rest on the documented case-by-case practice, not on a published standard.
blindSourceSummaries: Official 2026 Pride safety and travel guidance: visa requirements depend only on nationality, not gender identity — trans and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications; passports with a marker different from the birth-assigned sex or an 'X' marker are valid if officially issued, and no extra gender documents are required at the border. The country ranks #13 on a regional rights map for 2026.

A rights organisation's overview (March 2026): legal gender change still requires a medical expert letter, falling short of self-determination; the 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking 3-9 months; the self-identification act was withdrawn in July 2025; compensation was offered to people sterilised under earlier rules.

Official government material on combating anti-LGBTIQ+ discrimination and violence: over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence — 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people — and incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply per the 2023 national programme against discrimination and racism (in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation).

Official national announcements (laws in force 1 July 2025): a private member's bill puts discriminatory motive into law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, alongside expanded victims' rights and protection of victim data — the aggravating-factor mechanism in force since 1 July 2025.

Comparative rights data: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change legal but requires medical diagnosis, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only, discrimination illegal, employment and housing discrimination prohibited on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. High public support (52% support LGBT openness; ranked #2 of 121 regions as a 'good place').

News reporting (Apr 2026) citing police figures: 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year — up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022 — with reports about transgender people up 51% in a year (264 to 399); a national LGBTQ advocacy organisation calls it 'extremely worrying', noting only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination last year.

News reporting (Jul 2026): more than 70 people reported discrimination during the start of Pride via a reporting platform — mostly festival-goers and Pride march participants — with the platform warning the reports are 'only a fraction of the total'.

News reporting (Jun 2026): the capital broadened safer-spaces reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during Pride — landmark buildings, museums, archives, hotels plus a central reporting location — with 1.4 million visitors expected.

News reporting (Jun 2026): the mayor told the council the capital will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during Pride (police, enforcement and organiser agreements to act fast); recent Prides drew 25-45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports (vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation, serious assault), typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.

An international monitoring-frameworks page: national legislation contains no statutory definition of "hate crime", while police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through a dedicated police expertise centre.

A national human-rights lawyers' committee announced (22 Feb 2024) that it had advised the caretaker minister for legal protection on the placement of transgender detainees: no law or regulation currently governs their placement, which the committee calls worrying and undesirable. The note highlights the group's vulnerable position (international research documents human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence), the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees, and the relevance of regional human-rights standards, pointing to the full letter (21 Feb 2024).

A human-rights lawyers' committee letter (21 Feb 2024) documenting placement practice for transgender detainees: there is no law, regulation or official policy governing their placement — the penitentiary principles legislation only separates male and female detainees — and the prison service confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in municipal records together with case-by-case factors (gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, physical/mental health), while the custodial-institutions agency said it was drafting unpublished guidelines. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'extra-care facility' wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. The letter cites documented cases: a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing at arrival then moved to an extra-care facility wing; a 2016 parole-board appeals ruling on a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to a women's prison, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation while there; and 2017 and 2020 sentencing rulings treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. The committee asks the minister to create rules aligned with regional human-rights standards placing transgender detainees by gender identity.
